title: Post and Core Build-Ups: Rebuilding a Root-Canalled Tooth
metaTitle: Post and Core After a Root Canal: A Simple Guide
metaDescription: What a post and core build-up is, when it is used to support a crown on a heavily damaged root-canalled tooth, and what the procedure involves.
excerpt: A plain-language explanation of post and core build-ups: what they are, when they are needed, and how they support a crown.
heroImageAlt: A diagram of a tooth with a post placed in the root canal and a core build-up supporting a crown.
bodyHtml:
A post and core is a way of rebuilding a tooth that has lost a lot of structure after a root canal so that it can support a crown. The post is a small rod anchored into one of the cleaned root canals, and the core is the filling material built up around it to replace the missing part of the tooth and give the crown something solid to grip. Not everyone needs one; it is used mainly when too little natural tooth remains for a crown to hold on its own.

Why some teeth need a build-up

Teeth that require root canals are often already badly broken down by decay, a large old filling, or a fracture. After the canals are cleaned, there may not be enough healthy tooth left above the gumline to hold a crown securely. In that case, the tooth needs to be rebuilt first. A post and core provides that foundation: it restores enough bulk and retention for the crown to sit on, much like reinforcing and rebuilding a base before placing a cap on top.

The post and the core explained

It helps to think of the two parts separately:

  • The post is placed into a root canal space to anchor the restoration within the tooth. Posts are made from materials such as metal or tooth-coloured fibre, and the dentist chooses based on the tooth and the situation.
  • The core is the build-up material shaped around the post to recreate the missing portion of the tooth. Once the core is formed, it is prepared just like a natural tooth stump to receive the crown.

Together they turn a severely broken-down tooth into one that can be crowned.

When a post is not needed

A post is not automatically part of every root canal restoration. If a tooth still has a good amount of solid structure, a core build-up alone, or even a filling and crown without a separate post, may be enough. Front teeth and teeth with substantial remaining walls often do not require a post. The decision is individual and based on how much tooth is left, which tooth it is, and the forces it must withstand, so your dentist will assess what your tooth needs.

What the procedure involves

When a post and core is planned, the dentist prepares space within a root canal, places the post, and builds the core around it, then shapes everything to receive the crown. It is typically done as part of the restorative phase after the root canal itself is complete. As with any dental work, the goal is a strong, well-sealed foundation, and your dentist will explain the specific steps and materials they intend to use for your tooth.

Does placing a post weaken the tooth?

A post is used to help retain the restoration, not to strengthen the root itself, and preparing space for one is done carefully. Whether a post is worthwhile is a balance your dentist weighs for each tooth, choosing the approach most likely to give a stable, lasting result.

Will I feel the post and core?

Once the crown is placed over the build-up, the tooth is designed to function like a normal tooth for everyday chewing. The post and core are internal, supporting the crown from within, so you should not feel them separately.

How long does a post and core last?

When well made and protected by a properly fitted crown, a post and core can support a tooth for many years, though no restoration can be guaranteed to last forever. Good oral hygiene and regular dental visits help the tooth stay healthy over time.

Rebuilding your tooth

If a heavily damaged tooth needs rebuilding after a root canal, a general dentist can assess whether a post and core is the right approach and carry out the restoration.
